slides.0.title: Barossa Valley: Home of Old-Vine Shiraz
slides.0.subtitle: Level 1 · Module 3 · Lesson 1
slides.1.title: Barossa Valley: Essential Facts
slides.1.points.0: Location: 60 km northeast of Adelaide; altitude 270–550 m
slides.1.points.1: Climate: hot continental — average summer 34°C, very low rainfall
slides.1.points.2: Soil: sandy loam and clay loam; phylloxera-free (vines on own roots)
slides.1.points.3: Key variety: Shiraz (60%+ of Barossa plantings); also Grenache, Mourvèdre
slides.1.points.4: Old vine defining age: 35+ years = Barossa Old Vine; 70+ = Survivor Vine; 100+ = Ancestor Vine
slides.2.title: Why Are Old Vines So Precious?
slides.2.points.0: Deep roots: old vines reach 10–15 m underground, accessing minerals and moisture unavailable to young vines
slides.2.points.1: Self-regulating yield: old vines produce fewer grapes naturally — concentration increases dramatically
slides.2.points.2: SA phylloxera-free: because phylloxera never reached SA, vines grow on their own roots without grafting
slides.2.points.3: Australia's treasure: Barossa has the world's oldest commercially producing Shiraz vines — some over 170 years old
slides.3.title: Top Barossa Producers
slides.3.points.0: 🏆 Penfolds (Grange): Australia's most iconic wine; Barossa Shiraz as backbone
slides.3.points.1: 🌿 Henschke (Hill of Grace): single-vineyard, 130+ year old Eden Valley vines
slides.3.points.2: 🍷 Torbreck: specialist in ancient vine GSM blends
slides.3.points.3: 🦁 Two Hands: premium single-vineyard Shiraz across multiple SA regions
slides.3.points.4: 🌳 Elderton: Barossa family estate; Command Shiraz is benchmark
slides.4.question: Why does Barossa Valley have so many old vines that are over 100 years old?
slides.4.options.1: Phylloxera never reached SA, so vines can grow on their own roots and live for centuries
slides.4.options.2: The soil is too hard to replant vines
slides.4.options.3: No money was available for new plantings
slides.4.explanation: Phylloxera (a vine louse that devastated Europe's vineyards in the late 19th century) never spread to South Australia. This means Barossa vines were never killed off and replanted on grafted rootstock. Ungrafted own-rooted vines can live for well over a century, making Barossa home to some of the world's oldest producing vines.
slides.5.title: Lesson Summary
slides.5.points.0: Barossa's hot continental climate + phylloxera-free status = world's oldest Shiraz vines
slides.5.points.1: Old vine categories: Old Vine (35+), Survivor (70+), Ancestor (100+) years
slides.5.points.2: Top producers: Penfolds, Henschke, Torbreck — benchmarks of Barossa Shiraz
